analysis.one_liner: Requires regulations to cap U.S. carbon dioxide emissions at 1990 levels by 2000.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 148 cosponsors, including 13 Republicans, but was never given a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the President to issue final regulations, using existing federal agency authority, that hold total U.S. carbon dioxide emissions at their 1990 level by January 1, 2000. It would have required the EPA to evaluate progress every two years and forced the President to issue tougher rules if the first ones fell short. Citizens would be allowed to sue federal officials in court to enforce these duties. The bill sat in a House subcommittee and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to the effects of climate change — which the bill's own findings describe as more severe hurricanes and droughts, damage to agriculture, flooding of coastal areas, and saltwater intrusion into drinking water supplies [S3]. Stabilizing emissions at 1990 levels would have been achieved largely through energy efficiency and fuel switching, holding down long-term fuel costs [S3]. The bill's findings state that National Academy of Sciences and Office of Technology Assessment analyses found stabilization could be achieved at little or no cost, or even a net savings, to the economy [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President to promulgate final regulations, within two years of enactment, that achieve stabilization of U.S. carbon dioxide emissions at 1990 levels by January 1, 2000 [S2][S3].
Requires the EPA Administrator to evaluate progress every two years, and if the regulations will not achieve stabilization, requires the President to issue additional regulations that will [S2][S3].
Allows any U.S. citizen to sue federal officers in federal court for failing to perform non-discretionary duties under the Act, a backstop against inaction [S2][S3].

The bill's findings cite scientific assessments that climate change could increase the severity of hurricanes and droughts, hurt agriculture, flood coastal areas, and contaminate drinking water with saltwater — harms stabilization would work to avert [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the direct costs would fall on producers and users of coal, oil, and other fossil fuels, whose emissions would be capped; electric utilities burning fossil fuels would bear compliance costs, some portion of which would reach consumers through energy prices [S3]. The bill's own findings argue these costs would be small or negative overall, but that was contested by the industries affected.

drawbacks.text: The bill ordered the President to achieve stabilization using existing agency authorities but did not specify the regulatory tools, leaving industry, utilities, and consumers to face rules of uncertain design and cost [S3].

Compliance costs for coal, oil, and gas users and fossil-fired utilities would ultimately be passed at least partly to households through higher energy prices, even if the bill's cited studies found net economy-wide costs to be small [S3].
A hard statutory cap on total emissions set by 1992 law offered little flexibility if achieving it proved costlier than the studies cited in the findings predicted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — locking in a legal cap on the nation's largest greenhouse gas emissions with citizen enforcement — was large and long-lasting; the cost, per the studies cited in the bill itself, was estimated at little or no net cost to the economy, though energy-intensive industries and coal-dependent utilities would have borne real compliance costs and households would have seen some of those costs in prices. The main design weakness was that the bill set a target without choosing the tools to hit it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and stayed there without a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on April 2, 1992, and 148 House members signed on as cosponsors — 134 Democrats, 13 Republicans, and 1 independent [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction [S5].
On April 10, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where no further action was taken [S5].
No committee markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and fossil-fired electric utilities, which would have faced a statutory cap on carbon dioxide emissions, were better off because the bill never advanced; House members who opposed it were spared a recorded vote on 148-billpaper-strong bipartisan support.

for.name: Henry A. Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Global Climate Protection Act and organized original cosupport from over 100 House members on introduction day.

for.name: 148 House cosponsors
for.role: 134 of 267 House Democrats, 13 of 166 House Republicans, 1 of 2 House independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad bipartisan support in the House.

against.name: John D. Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a markup or committee vote; the bill was sent to the Energy and Power Subcommittee and went no further.

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Power
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from April 10, 1992 onward without any action, hearing, or vote recorded in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 134 Democrats, 13 Republicans, and 1 independent cosponsored — and the bill was never voted on, so no roll-call split ever materialized; it died in committee under a Democratic chair.

industries.note: A statutory cap on total U.S. carbon dioxide emissions, to be reached by 2000, would directly constrain the production and use of fossil fuels — the main source of those emissions. Blocking the bill preserved the industry's unrestricted emissions trajectory.

Coal- and oil-burning power plants are among the largest carbon dioxide sources, so stabilization regulations using EPA and other agency authority would have required costly changes or fuel switching. Keeping the bill in subcommittee avoided that compliance burden.

industries.industry: Energy efficiency and renewable energy sectors
industries.note: A hard cap on total emissions would have created demand for efficiency improvements and low-carbon energy as the least-cost compliance paths. The bill cited analyses finding stabilization achievable at little or no net economic cost, implying substitution toward these sectors.
